claim_verdicts.evidence: git-log, path limiting: "[--] <path>... Show only commits that are enough to explain how the files that match the specified paths came to be. See History Simplification below for details and other simplification modes." and "Paths may need to be prefixed with -- to separate them from options or the revision range, when confusion arises." The `--` half is exact. "Commits that changed that path" is exact only for a linear history; default history simplification prunes TREESAME parents of merges, so on a merged history some commits that touched the path are not printed.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: `git log -- <path>` narrows the history to the commits Git keeps as the explanation of that path — in a straight-line history, exactly the commits that changed it; the `--` separates paths from branch names, which otherwise can be read either way.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-log: "--oneline: This is a shorthand for --pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit used together." and DESCRIPTION: "The output is given in reverse chronological order by default." The captured run at stage-0 shows one line per commit, abbreviated id then subject: "c812dbd Explain the rounding".

git-blame DESCRIPTION: "Annotates each line in the given file with information from the revision which last modified the line." The captured run shows the default format carrying author and author date: "b3472f64 (Mai Anh 2026-02-05 12:00:00 +0700 9) echo $(( (total / 1000000) * 1000000 ))".

git-blame: "-w Ignore whitespace when comparing the parent's version and the child's to find where the lines came from" — i.e. whitespace-only edits do count by default; "The origin of lines is automatically followed across whole-file renames (currently there is no option to turn the rename-following off)"; "-M Detect moved or copied lines within a file" and "-C In addition to -M, detect lines moved or copied from other files that were modified in the same commit."

git-reset: "Set the current branch head (HEAD) to point at <commit>." "The <mode> must be one of the following (default --mixed)". --soft: "Leave your working tree files and the index unchanged." --mixed: "Leave your working directory unchanged. Update the index to match the new HEAD, so nothing will be staged." --hard: "Overwrite all files and directories with the version from <commit>... Update the index to match the new HEAD, so nothing will be staged."

git-revert DESCRIPTION: "Given one or more existing commits, revert the changes that the related patches introduce, and record some new commits that record them." Execution at stage-0 confirms the reverted commit stays and the branch grows: `git log --oneline -3` after the revert prints "e415afb Revert \"Round the total down to millions\" / 57a2d53 Add a README / c812dbd Explain the rounding", with b3472f6 still on the branch below.

git-revert: "--no-edit: With this option, git revert will not start the commit message editor." git-switch: "-c <new-branch> ... Create a new branch named <new-branch> starting at <start-point> before switching to the branch"; "<start-point>: The starting point for the new branch"; "-q, --quiet: Quiet, suppress feedback messages."

git-reflog DESCRIPTION: "Reference logs, or 'reflogs', record when the tips of branches and other references were updated in the local repository"; "The reflog covers all recent actions, and in addition the HEAD reflog records branch switching"; "git reflog show accepts any of the options accepted by git log" — so `-4` is git-log's "-<number>: Limit the output to the first <number> commits". gitrevisions: "master@{1} is the immediate prior value of master while master@{5} is the 5th prior value".

git-reflog DESCRIPTION: "Reference logs, or 'reflogs', record when the tips of branches and other references were updated in the local repository", and "master@{one.week.ago} means 'where master used to point to one week ago in this local repository'". Nothing in git-clone/git-push transfers reflogs; the captured run of recover-with-reflog.sh at stage-0 recovers 57a2d53 with no network command in the script.

git-gc: "--prune: Prune loose objects older than date (default is 2 weeks ago, overridable by the config variable gc.pruneExpire)"; gc.reflogExpire: "git reflog expire removes reflog entries older than this time; defaults to 90 days"; gc.reflogExpireUnreachable: "...defaults to 30 days", with the note that such entries "are generally created as a result of using git commit --amend or git rebase and are the commits prior to the amend or rebase occurring". So the commit is not removed at once.

git-commit --amend: "Replace the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit." and "You should understand the implications of rewriting history if you amend a commit that has already been published." git-gc's gc.reflogExpireUnreachable describes the pre-amend commits as reflog entries "not reachable from the current tip", which is exactly "unreachable from the branch tip but still named by the reflog".

gitrevisions: "A suffix ~<n> to a revision parameter means the commit object that is the <n>th generation ancestor of the named commit object, following only the first parents. I.e. <rev>~3 is equivalent to <rev>^^^ which is equivalent to <rev>^1^1^1."

git-log: "--grep=<pattern>: Limit the commits output to ones with a log message that matches the <pattern> regular expression"; "-<number>, -n <number>, --max-count=<number>: Limit the output to the first <number> commits that would be shown"; PRETTY FORMATS list %h abbreviated commit hash, %H commit hash, %ad author date (respects --date=), %s subject, %n newline; "--date=short shows only the date, but not the time, in YYYY-MM-DD format". The captured run prints "b3472f6 2026-02-05".

git-blame --abbrev: "Instead of using the default 7+1 hexadecimal digits as the abbreviated object name, use <m>+1 digits..." — blame's default is 8 characters. git-log's --oneline is "--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit", which in this small repository abbreviates to 7. The captured run shows both in one output: blame line "b3472f64 (Mai Anh ...)" and log line "b3472f6 Round the total down to millions".

outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/blame-and-log.txt: the log block lists exactly c812dbd, b3472f6, d915e63; the blame block has 9 lines, of which the lesson shows only the last (8 elided, matching "the eight earlier lines"); the revert block reads "e415afb Revert ... / 57a2d53 Add a README / c812dbd Explain the rounding" and ends with "ok". git-playground/build-history.sh makes six commits on main (price list, total.sh+test.sh, second product, rounding, explanation, README).
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang at stage-0 (tag object 664d38a -> commit ff911b0): outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/blame-and-log.txt, git-playground/build-history.sh

claim_verdicts.evidence: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/recover-with-reflog.txt: "where the branch points now: 57a2d53 Add a README"; "after git reset --hard HEAD~2: b3472f6 Round the total down to millions"; "57a2d53 HEAD@{1}: checkout: moving from main to reflog-demo"; and after the reset onto reflog-demo@{1}: "57a2d53 Add a README / c812dbd Explain the rounding / b3472f6 Round the total down to millions".

The captured reflog block at stage-0 reads "b3472f6 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2 / 57a2d53 HEAD@{1}: checkout: moving from main to reflog-demo / 57a2d53 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from feature/currency to main / 2f97b1c HEAD@{3}: commit: Print the total in đồng", while scripts/git/recover-with-reflog.sh line 10 runs `git switch --quiet -c reflog-demo main` — so the label is `checkout:` for a move made by switch. git-reflog: "the HEAD reflog records branch switching".

git-push, NOTE ABOUT FAST-FORWARDS: "When an update changes a branch ... that used to point at commit A to point at another commit B, it is called a fast-forward update if and only if B is a descendant of A"; "a non-fast-forward update will lose history"; "The command by default does not allow an update that is not a fast-forward to prevent such loss of history"; "git push --force is a method reserved for a case where you do mean to lose history."

git-playground/build-history.sh exports GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/EMAIL and GIT_COMMITTER_NAME/EMAIL ('Mai Anh') and its save() sets GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE per commit; scripts/git/blame-and-log.sh lines 24-25 export both dates as 2026-02-10T09:00:00+07:00 before the revert; scripts/git/recover-with-reflog.sh creates no commit (switch, reset, log, reflog only), so it needs no date pinning. Same inputs therefore yield the same ids as the captured outputs.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang at stage-0: git-playground/build-history.sh, scripts/git/blame-and-log.sh, scripts/git/recover-with-reflog.sh

claim_verdicts.evidence: Documentation supports the recommendation as conditioned. git-push: "a non-fast-forward update will lose history" and "The command by default does not allow an update that is not a fast-forward to prevent such loss of history." git-revert records "some new commits", so a revert is a fast-forward for everyone else. The lesson states the condition ("Once a commit is on the server"), so it is not an unconditional ranking.

git-rebase, RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE: "Rebasing (or any other form of rewriting) a branch that others have based work on is a bad idea: anyone downstream of it is forced to manually fix their history. ... The real fix, however, would be to avoid rebasing the upstream in the first place." git-commit --amend: "You should understand the implications of rewriting history if you amend a commit that has already been published."

gitglossary, object: "The unit of storage in Git. It is uniquely identified by the SHA-1 of its contents. Consequently, an object cannot be changed." object name: "The unique identifier of an object ... usually represented by a 40 character hexadecimal string." commit object: contains "parents, committer, author, date and the tree object" — so changing message or parent changes the contents and therefore the id.

git-rebase, INTERACTIVE MODE: "If you want to fold two or more commits into one, replace the command 'pick' for the second and subsequent commits with 'squash' or 'fixup'." — one commit carrying the combined change. RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE calls rebase "any other form of rewriting" of a branch, and git-reflog records "when the tips of branches ... were updated in the local repository", which is the entry from before the rebase.
claim_verdicts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase (INTERACTIVE MODE, RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE); https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog

claim_verdicts.evidence: Both scripts at stage-0 have line 7 "/repo/git-playground/build-history.sh >/dev/null" followed by "cd /tmp/git-playground". scripts/up.sh runs only ./scripts/dev-secrets.sh and `docker compose up -d --build --wait`, then prints URLs — it never touches git-playground. build-history.sh commits six times on main before switching to feature/shipping and feature/currency, and ends "built $repo with $(git rev-list --count main) commits on main".

issues.text: Too strong for the general case. git-log documents path limiting as "Show only commits that are enough to explain how the files that match the specified paths came to be. See History Simplification" — under the default simplification a merged history can hide commits that did change the path. The statement is exact only because the playground's main is a straight line, which the lesson does not say.
issues.quote: `git log --oneline -- total.sh` prints only the commits that changed that file
issues.fix: Write "prints the commits Git keeps as the explanation of that file — in a straight-line history like this one, the commits that changed it", and match the Core-concepts line ("the history narrowed to the commits that changed one path") to the same wording. Add the qualifier to claim 1 in .meta.json.

issues.text: The sentence gives --grep a job it does not have. Per git-log, "--grep=<pattern>: Limit the commits output to ones with a log message that matches" — it keeps every matching commit; it is "-<number>: Limit the output to the first <number> commits that would be shown" (here `-1`) that reduces the set to the newest one. Claim 13 in the ledger splits the two correctly; the lesson sentence does not.
issues.quote: `--grep` picks the newest commit whose message matches
issues.fix: Write "`--grep` keeps only the commits whose message matches and `-1` takes the newest of them".

issues.text: Unconditional where the documentation is not. git-gc prunes loose objects "older than date (default is 2 weeks ago...)" and gc.reflogExpire "removes reflog entries older than this time; defaults to 90 days" (30 days for entries not reachable from the tip). Claim 10 is careful ("is not removed at once"); the lesson promises the commits simply "stay", which is what a reader will remember a year later.
issues.quote: the commits it pointed at stay in the repository, still reachable through the reflog
issues.fix: Write "the commits it pointed at stay in the repository for months, still reachable through the reflog" (or "...stay until Git's housekeeping eventually clears what no name and no reflog entry reaches").

issues.text: Unlisted claim about the example system: nothing in the ledger states that up.sh is safe to run again. It is true at stage-0 — scripts/dev-secrets.sh writes .env and secrets/lab_key only inside `if [ ! -f ... ]` guards and `docker compose up -d --build --wait` converges on a lab already up — but a second run does rebuild images, so "changes nothing" describes the end state, not the command. The same sentence was flagged in the three sibling git lessons.
issues.quote: run `scripts/up.sh` (running it twice changes nothing)
issues.fix: Write "(running it again when the lab is already up leaves you in the same place)" and extend claim 24 in .meta.json with the idempotence, naming the `if [ ! -f ... ]` guards in dev-secrets.sh and `docker compose up -d --build --wait`.

issues.text: The diagram breaks the convention the paragraph under it states. `main` and `reflog-demo` are drawn as separate dotted name nodes, but `revert-demo` is folded into the commit node's own label, so the only branch created in the first script looks like part of a commit's text rather than a name pointing at it.
issues.quote: V["e415afb revert-demo: revert the rounding commit"]
issues.fix: Relabel the commit node "e415afb Revert the rounding commit" and add a dotted name node for the branch, e.g. `RD(["revert-demo"]) -.-> V`, so all three names are drawn the same way.

junior.reviewer: review-junior (prompt 05, claude-opus-5; fresh session; known_vocab = the 41 terms supplied with the task, process .. conflict, plus the five-line summary of foundation.l2.git-merge-vs-rebase; lesson .en.md and .quiz.json only; .meta.json and the technical block not read before writing this; replaces an earlier junior block written against a previous draft)

issues.text: "push" is the word the whole revert-vs-reset choice hangs on, and it arrives already in use. I can guess it means "send my commits somewhere", but nothing tells me what the shared repository does with one, so later I cannot follow why one push goes through and another "is refused".
issues.quote: every other copy gains a commit when you push it to the shared repository everyone works from
issues.fix: Gloss it at first use: change to "...when you push it — send your new commits to the shared repository everyone works from — every other copy gains a commit."

issues.text: "the server" appears for the first time here, after the text has been calling the same thing "the shared repository everyone works from". I stop to work out whether they are one place or two, and section 6 then says "the server's copy" as well.
issues.quote: Once a commit is on the server, revert is the safe shape: it adds, where reset asks every other copy to forget.
issues.fix: Use one name throughout: replace "on the server" here with "in the shared repository", and in section 6 replace "behind the server's copy" / "the server dropping commits" with "behind the shared copy" / "the shared repository dropping commits".

issues.text: I cannot reconstruct why naming b3472f6 means "back two commits": section 4 never says where the branch is standing when you run this, so the distance two comes from nowhere. The script later uses HEAD~2 instead of the id, which makes it harder, not easier.
issues.quote: `git reset --hard b3472f6` instead moves your current branch name back two commits and makes your files match it
issues.fix: Say where the name starts: "`git reset --hard b3472f6`, run while the branch stands two commits later, moves your current branch name back onto `b3472f6` and makes your files match it".

issues.text: The prose says the script "switches to a throwaway branch" but never says the branch is created at `main`. That is exactly the fact quiz q5 asks me to use (whether `main` still rounds), and I cannot get it from the prose — only by decoding `-c revert-demo main` myself.
issues.quote: Then the script switches to a throwaway branch and reverts, where `--no-edit` keeps the message Git writes
issues.fix: Say what the line does: "Then the script creates a throwaway branch `revert-demo` at `main`, switches to it and reverts there, so only that branch gains the new commit; `--no-edit` keeps the message Git writes...".

issues.text: Nothing explains `@{1}`. In the output I read `HEAD@{0}` and `HEAD@{1}` as labels printed by the command; then a command types `reflog-demo@{1}` and I have to guess that the number means "one move back" and that each name has its own numbering. Without that guess the last command is magic, and the Try it "Expected result" repeats the same notation.
issues.quote: The last command reads a second log, `reflog-demo@{1}`, the branch's own record of where it stood before the reset
issues.fix: Add one sentence after the `HEAD@{1}` explanation: "`@{1}` means one move back in that name's own reflog, so `reflog-demo@{1}` is where the branch stood before the reset, just as `HEAD@{1}` is where `HEAD` stood."

issues.text: The diagram shows three commits in a line with `main` on the last, so I count three; section 2 told me `main` has six, and nothing marks the earlier three as left out. `c812dbd "Explain the rounding"` is a node I never meet again in section 4's prose, so I cannot say why it is drawn.
issues.quote: Solid arrows run from a commit to the one after it; dotted arrows are names, and one line of the reflog
issues.fix: Add to that sentence: "only the last three of the six commits on `main` are drawn; `c812dbd`, the commit that added the comment above the rounding line, sits between them."

issues.text: The second misconception is one I would hold, but the correction is the first place the push mechanism is explained, and it explains it with the two words I do not have (push, server). So the sentence that is supposed to settle the difference is the hardest one in the lesson.
issues.quote: the reset leaves your branch behind the server's copy so the push is refused, because accepting it would mean the server dropping commits it already has
issues.fix: Put the mechanism where the choice is made: in section 4, after "reset asks every other copy to forget", add "a shared repository refuses a push that would drop commits it already has".

issues.text: "pulled" appears nowhere in the lesson. I can guess it means "already have a copy of", but I am guessing in the one question where the whole point is which copies already hold a commit.
issues.quote: so on a branch other people have already pulled, either one is equally safe to push
issues.fix: Reword to "on a branch other people already have a copy of", matching the wording section 4 uses.

issues.text: `$( ... )` is used twice in the scripts and never explained. The prose tells me the effect ("hands that commit to `git log -1`") but not the notation, so when I read the second script's last line I cannot tell it is the same trick.
issues.quote: git log -1 --format='%h %ad%n%n%s' --date=short "$(git log --format=%H -1 --grep='Round the total')"
issues.fix: Add to the sentence that explains `--grep` and `%h`: "`$( ... )` runs the inner command first and pastes its output into the outer one".

issues.text: `>/dev/null` sits on the revert line and the prose never mentions it, so I wonder whether it is part of reverting or changes what the revert does.
issues.quote: git revert --no-edit "$(git log --format=%H -1 --grep='Round the total')" >/dev/null
issues.fix: Add to the `--no-edit` sentence: "and `>/dev/null` only hides the revert's own progress line, so the output below starts at the log".

issues.text: Step 1 tells me to run `scripts/up.sh` but not what it is or why it comes first; the reassurance about rebuilding is attached to the two git scripts instead. I would run it not knowing what I am waiting for.
issues.quote: run `scripts/up.sh` (running it twice changes nothing), then run `scripts/git/blame-and-log.sh`
issues.fix: Say what it does in the same clause, e.g. "run `scripts/up.sh`, which puts the example system in its starting state (running it twice changes nothing)".

issues.text: "the playground" turns up in section 5 and in Try it, but section 2 called it "a throwaway repository". Reading that a playground "made moves" stopped me twice — I was not sure whether a third thing had entered the lesson.
issues.quote: The two lines below are older moves the playground made before this branch existed
issues.fix: Use one name: either call it "the throwaway repository" in both places, or introduce the word once in section 2 ("a throwaway repository — the playground").

issues.text: The reset bullet defines reset, then three modes, then introduces staging inside a dash, in one sentence. I re-read it three times and still could not hold `--soft` and `--mixed` apart, partly because neither is used anywhere later in the lesson.
issues.quote: `--soft` moves the name alone, `--mixed` also unmarks the changes you had staged — the ones marked to go into the next commit — while leaving the files themselves untouched
issues.fix: Split into two sentences: one saying what reset is, one listing the three modes with the staging gloss moved to the end ("staged changes are the ones marked to go into the next commit").

issues.text: Summary line 4 is about `--soft`/`--mixed`/`--hard`, but only `--hard` is ever shown or used; the other two exist in one Core concepts clause. Coming back to the summary, line 4 feels like a line from a lesson I did not read, unlike amend and squash which at least say plainly that they are not run here.
issues.quote: `--soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` decide how far a reset reaches: the name alone, the staging marks too, or your files as well.
issues.fix: Do for the modes what the amend/squash bullet does: add to the reset bullet in Core concepts "only `--hard` is run in this lesson's scripts; you meet the other two so you recognise the words".

issues.text: The explanation for wrong option c leaves me worse off: it says the job belongs to "the names that track the shared copy", an idea the lesson never mentions. I now think there is a second kind of name I was supposed to know about.
issues.quote: That job belongs to the names that track the shared copy; the reflog is written by your own commands and never travels between repositories.
issues.fix: Drop the unexplained idea: "Your repository does have to remember something about the shared copy, but that is not the reflog — the reflog is written by your own commands and never travels between repositories."

issues.text: Option a is the lesson's own sentence with the words shuffled, so I chose it by recognising the phrasing rather than by understanding ids. The three wrong options all add a reason; the right one is the only bare statement.
issues.quote: They are one commit: `git blame` and `git log` shorten the same id to different lengths.
issues.fix: Reword option a away from the lesson's wording and give it a reason too, e.g. "One commit: the full id is longer than both strings, and each command prints as much of it as it likes."

issues.text: Option a repeats the third "Beginners often think" bullet almost word for word ("an indentation change or a reformatting counts as touching it"), so I could pick it from memory of that line without deciding anything about the teammate's claim.
issues.quote: Only that one commit last touched every line, and a reformatting or a re-indentation does that without changing what the file does.
issues.fix: Reword option a so it is not the bullet's sentence, e.g. "Only that one commit is the last to have touched each line, which a whole-file formatting change would also produce."
